prompt.context: Your client is Tacotle Co., a leading national fast casual restaurant with $420M in revenue in 2014. Over the five years preceding 2014, Tacotle has experienced steady revenue growth and industry-leading profitability. For the first time in its 15-year history, Tacotle has experienced three straight quarters of EBITDA erosion.
prompt.question: Tacotle's CEO has hired you to explore what is causing profits to drop and what can be done to reverse the tide.

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal — a specific profit target?
clarifying_info.a: No specific milestones; the client is looking for positive annual profit growth in the short term.
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization — a proxy for operating profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any major changes in the competitive landscape?
clarifying_info.a: No major competitors have entered or exited; no new substitutes have been introduced; Tacotle maintains a 30% market share by revenue.

clarifying_info.q: How is the overall market performing?
clarifying_info.a: The market is mature and growing at the same rate as GDP.
Customers are beginning to stress the importance of ingredient quality and order customization.

clarifying_info.q: How did average time to serve a customer change?
clarifying_info.a: Average service time increased from approximately 1 minute to approximately 3.5 minutes.

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. quarterly revenue and EBITDA
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing quarterly Revenue and EBITDA (in $M) from Q1 2012 through Q4 2014, with EBITDA % labeled above each bar pair.
exhibits.data: EBITDA % by quarter: Q1–Q4 2012: 44%, 45%, 44%, 46%; Q1–Q4 2013: 45%, 45%, 44%, 46%; Q1–Q4 2014: 39%, 40%, 39%, 40%. Revenue and EBITDA bars show a spike in Q1 2014 followed by steady decline through Q4 2014.

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. avg. revenue per order
exhibits.shows: Line chart showing average revenue per order over time, with the y-axis ranging from $3.00 to $5.50.
exhibits.data: Average price was approximately $4.05 in 2013 and rose to approximately $5.25 in 2014.

exhibits.title: Tacotle Co. income statement
exhibits.shows: Annual income statement for 2012, 2013, and 2014 with revenue and expense line items.

exhibits.title: Results of 2013 Tacotle Co. customer survey
exhibits.shows: Bar chart comparing customer-rated Importance vs. Tacotle Performance across seven attributes on a 0–5 scale, based on the 2013 survey.
exhibits.data: Attributes (Importance / Performance): Quality 4.8/3.4, Speed of Service 4.7/3.3, Consistency of Product 4.5/3.1, Has a drive-through 4.5/-, Restaurant Cleanliness -/-, Friendliness of Staff -/-, Ample Seating -/-. Tacotle lags notably on Quality; meets or exceeds expectations on most other dimensions.

exhibits.title: Results of 2014 Tacotle Co. customer survey
exhibits.shows: Bar chart comparing customer-rated Importance vs. Tacotle Performance across seven attributes on a 0–5 scale, based on the 2014 survey. The attribute order has changed relative to Exhibit D.
exhibits.data: Attributes listed in new order (Importance / Performance): Speed of Service 4.8/3.5, Quality 4.7/4.6, Has a drive-through 4.5/-, Consistency of Product 4.5/3.4, Restaurant Cleanliness -/-, Friendliness of Staff -/-, Ample Seating -/-. Speed of Service is now ranked most important and is below expectations; Consistency of Product has also dropped below expectations.

framework: Declining EBITDA: decompose into market conditions vs. Tacotle-specific operations
Market Conditions: shrinking market? increased competition? shift in customer preferences?
Revenue: price change? volume/units sold change? product mix shift?
Costs: COGS (variable — ingredients, distribution); Labor (variable); Fixed costs (overhead, PP&E, SG&A, marketing)
Synthesis: identify which lever(s) moved and trace root cause

questions.prompt: What do you observe in Exhibit A, and what hypotheses does it generate?
questions.guidance: Revenue spiked in Q1 2014 then declined steadily. EBITDA remained roughly flat despite the revenue spike because EBITDA margin compressed sharply (from ~45% to ~39%). A strong candidate hypothesizes that either prices or volume increased but costs rose faster, then asks to see the income statement and average price data to decompose further.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits B and C, how did the total number of orders sold change from 2013 to 2014?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Units = Revenue / Avg. price per unit for each year and compare. Result shows revenue increased but unit volume fell — demonstrating that the revenue spike was price-driven, not volume-driven. Candidate should then ask why prices were raised and why units continued to fall.

math.setup: Units sold = Revenue / Average price per unit. Use 2013 revenue $377M (round to $380M) and avg price $4.05 (round to $4). Use 2014 revenue $420M and avg price $5.25.
math.answer: Units sold decreased by approximately 15 million orders (~16%) despite a revenue increase, confirming the revenue spike was entirely price-driven.

questions.prompt: What does Exhibit C reveal about cost drivers, and what is the root cause of EBITDA erosion?
questions.guidance: COGS nearly doubled from $54M (2013) to $96M (2014) while all other cost lines were essentially flat. EBITDA went from $170M to $169M — flat — because the price increase was fully offset by the COGS increase. The candidate should name COGS as the primary driver and hypothesize that a menu/ingredient change caused it.

steps: COGS as % of revenue 2014: $96M / $420M = 23% — nearly doubled as a share of revenue
math.answer: COGS nearly doubled in dollar terms and rose from ~14% to ~23% of revenue, fully offsetting the price-driven revenue gain and causing EBITDA margin to compress ~5 pp.

questions.prompt: What do Exhibits D and E tell you about operations and the effectiveness of the menu change?
questions.guidance: Exhibit D (2013 pre-change): Tacotle lagged on Quality but met or exceeded expectations elsewhere. Exhibit E (2014 post-change): Quality improved and now meets expectations, but Speed of Service became the top-ranked attribute by importance AND fell below expectations. Consistency of Product also fell below expectations. The net effect is an overall decrease in customer satisfaction. Candidate should recognize the menu change — adding customization and higher-quality ingredients — solved one problem (Quality) while creating two new ones (Speed, Consistency), driving the unit-volume decline.

brainstorming.prompt: List at least five cost drivers specific to the fast casual restaurant industry, broken down by fixed and variable costs.

recommendation: Scale back the menu changes implemented in 2014 — reduce the number of topping options and customization complexity to restore speed and consistency of service.

The menu change is the root cause: it nearly doubled COGS, degraded service speed from ~1 minute to ~3.5 minutes, reduced consistency, and drove a net decline in customer satisfaction that is eroding unit volume quarter over quarter.
risks: Scaling back too aggressively could reduce 'Quality' scores back below customer expectations, eliminating the one gain from the change.
Reversing the menu may disrupt supplier relationships and require divesting assets purchased for the new menu at a loss.
A scale-back that does not explicitly target margin improvement could shrink both revenue and profit, effectively downsizing the company.
next_steps: Conduct more detailed, focused customer surveys to identify the minimal set of customization/quality improvements customers value most.
Design a partial menu scale-back that cuts the highest-cost, lowest-satisfaction-impact items while preserving the quality perception gain.
Pilot the revised menu at a small number of locations before a national rollout to validate speed, consistency, and COGS impact.
